title: Twenty key words
hookLine: karma in a caption, nirvana for a quiet beach: you already speak a little Pali
tomorrow: what does a mother guarding her only child have to do with strangers?

cards: Somebody cuts the coffee line, then drops his cup on the way out, and a stranger mutters: karma. A quiet beach gets called nirvana in a caption. Those are Sanskrit spellings, and the everyday meanings have drifted.
But the Pali words underneath them, kamma and nibbana, are already in your ear. Add twenty days of chanting and a few years of lessons, and you know more Pali than you think.
Today you count it, and then you put it to work on a bad afternoon.

teach.b: Here they are, in small handfuls. The ache and the ease: dukkha, the sting of things not being right; sukha, ease. The mind: citta, heart and mind in one word; sati, remembering to notice.
What you do: kamma, intentional action, not fate; dana, giving; sila, good conduct; bhavana, growing the mind.
The four boundless ones: metta, goodwill; karuna, compassion; mudita, gladness at someone else's good; upekkha, a steady, even mind, which isn't the same as not caring.

How things are: anicca, impermanent; anatta, not-self. Where it leads: samadhi, a collected mind; panna, wisdom; nibbana, the going-out of greed, hatred and delusion. And the three you chant: Buddha, dhamma, sangha.
Now an ordinary bad day. A comment on your work that stings. That's dukkha, and naming it loosens it a little.

Sati catches the spiral: the fourth redraw, the replay in the shower. Metta turns around and faces you, the way you'd talk to a friend. Upekkha lets the comment be one opinion, not the weather for the week.
And kamma says the next stroke is still yours to make.

how: Pali words like dukkha, metta, sati and kamma are used in Dhamma talks and Buddhist classes in many languages, often left untranslated because each holds more than any one English word.

games.q: words you know — tap the pairs.
p: the sting of things not being right

s: kamma means fate: what happens to you was always going to happen
kamma is intentional action. what you do with intention shapes what comes, and the next action is still yours.
upekkha means not caring what happens
upekkha is a steady, even mind, one of the four boundless ones beside metta and karuna, not indifference.
citta covers both heart and mind
one Pali word where English needs two.

games.q: your friend bombs a test she didn't study for and sighs, 'it's my karma, i'm cursed.' which reply fits the Pali word?
o: yep, fate. nothing you could have done.
kamma is what you do with intention, so the next test is still yours to shape.
it's probably something from a past life catching up with you.
games.why: kamma is intentional action, not fate or a curse. the word points forward: what you choose now shapes what comes.

practice: Hold up both hands. On each finger, say one Pali word you know and what it means, ten in all, no peeking. Then rest your hands, and let the one that's most useful this week be the one you sit with.

wordCard.voice: Twenty key words: dukkha to nibbana, metta to sati. Not a vocabulary test. Handles on a life.

carryVoice: Your line: words you know now. A few of them are already doing their job. That's day twenty-one of the block.
